title: Sample complexity of proper PAC learning
formal: Historical question, resolved: can the extra log(1/ε) factor be removed from the worst-case proper PAC sample bound for every binary concept class? Equivalently, is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty finite concept class H of VC dimension d≥1 admits proper realizable PAC learning from at most ⌈C(d+ln(1/δ))/ε⌉ independent labeled examples, for every 0<ε<1/8 and 0<δ<1/100? The answer is no: some classes require Ω((d ln(1/ε)+ln(1/δ))/ε) examples from every proper learner, even when arbitrary computation and internal randomness are allowed.
context:
An improper learner may output a Boolean classifier outside the given class. Hanneke’s general PAC bound removes the logarithm in that setting. Requiring the output to lie inside the original class can increase the number of examples even when computation is unrestricted.

The 2017 conference conclusion listed necessity of the logarithm as open. In the October 2018 journal version, footnote 2 states that it is sometimes necessary for proper learners. The old conference sentence therefore does not support retaining this as an open problem.

Theorem 11 of the COLT 2020 paper gives classes with proper sample complexity Ω((d ln(1/ε)+ln(1/δ))/ε), including finite-domain versions with sufficiently large auxiliary class parameter. Its introduction describes earlier awareness of the basic separation as folklore; this card does not attribute first discovery to the 2020 theorem.

The same paper gives a log-free bound for SVM learning of halfspaces in the realizable setting. Such class-specific positive results coexist with the worst-class lower bound and do not contradict it.
why: Separates the statistical cost of predicting accurately from the additional requirement of expressing the predictor within a prescribed class. The resolution shows that representation constraints alone can increase sample complexity, independently of running time.
status_note: Read the original classical question, the October 2018 journal correction and COLT 2020 Theorem 11 with the finite-domain part of its Appendix C construction. Matched properness, arbitrary distributions, internal randomization and worst-case sample count. The finite hard class can depend on accuracy; no uniform asymptotic lower bound for every fixed finite class is claimed. The source’s suggested quantum task was removed rather than promoted to a new question.

sentences: A proper learner must always return a hypothesis from the known concept class.
The historical question asks whether this restriction can force an additional logarithmic factor in sample complexity.
The answer is yes for some classes, even with randomized learners and unlimited computation.
The 2018 journal version acknowledges this, and a 2020 theorem supplies matching worst-case lower bounds with finite-domain constructions.
Other classes, including halfspaces, can still attain the smaller proper-learning bound.

definitions:
Let X be any nonempty finite set and H⊆{0,1}^X a nonempty set of Boolean functions. The class is known to the learner. Its VC dimension d is the greatest size of a subset S⊆X for which every labeling S→{0,1} is the restriction of some h∈H. The source uses finite Boolean-string domains; any finite X can be encoded injectively in {0,1}ⁿ with all hypotheses extended by the same fixed label on unused strings, preserving the VC dimension and the lower-bound task on distributions supported on X.

An unknown target h* belongs to H. An arbitrary unknown distribution P on X generates m independent examples (X₁,h*(X₁)),…,(X_m,h*(X_m)), with each Xᵢ drawn from P. A proper learner is a possibly randomized rule that, given these examples and ε,δ, always returns a hypothesis ĥ∈H. It may depend on H,ε,δ, but not on P or h* except through the sample. Its internal randomness is independent of the examples. The requirement is Pr[P({x:ĥ(x)≠h*(x)})≤ε]≥1−δ for every P and every h*∈H, with probability over samples and learner randomness. There are no membership queries, quantum examples or additional unlabeled data. There is no time bound, no representation-efficiency requirement and no charge for evaluating hypotheses; only the number of independent labeled examples is counted.

For fixed H,ε,δ, M_prop(H,ε,δ) is the smallest integer m≥0 for which such a learner exists. A learner that uses at most m examples on every run can be viewed as using exactly m and ignoring unused examples, so this is a worst-case sample budget, not an expectation or a stopping-time average. Properness is required of all outputs. The learner need not be consistent with its observed sample; restricting to an arbitrary empirical-risk minimizer would be a narrower algorithm class and would not prove a lower bound against all proper learners. Output outside H is disallowed even when it predicts the target well.

The proposed constant C is independent of H, |X|, d, ε and δ. The classical upper bound O((d ln(1/ε)+ln(1/δ))/ε) has such universal constants. The later finite-domain lower bound states that a universal a>0 exists such that for each d≥1 and admissible ε,δ there is a finite class of VC dimension d with M_prop≥a(d ln(1/ε)+ln(1/δ))/ε. The class may depend on the accuracy; it is not asserted that one fixed finite class incurs the full logarithmic penalty as ε tends to zero. Theorem 11 supplies finite classes with arbitrarily large dual Helly number, and its Appendix C verifies the finite construction; choosing that auxiliary parameter sufficiently large gives the stated worst-class conclusion. Its additional infinite-class result is not needed to refute the universal finite-class bound. Logarithms here are natural; changing their base changes universal constants only.
answer_criterion: The historical negative resolution requires a lower bound against every proper learner for some concept classes, not merely an example of a bad ERM rule. The published lower bound matches the general proper-learning upper bound in its d ln(1/ε) and ln(1/δ) terms and excludes a universal log-free bound. It does not say that all classes incur this penalty, nor that computational hardness is responsible.
